lesson.title: Asking Questions
lesson.subtitle: was, wo, wer, wann — pure cognates, verb-first questions, zero do-support

foreshadow.line: One warning before you go: there is a little three-letter word that undoes everything you just learned about where the verb sits. You have not met it. It is coming.

hook.title: The W-Word Family Reunion
hook.content: German question words are not vocabulary to memorize — they are your own W-words with the h shaved off. was ↔ what, wo ↔ where, wer ↔ who, wann ↔ when, wohin ↔ whither. English spelled the old hw- as wh; German spelled it w and let the h go. One trap is built into the family: WER asks who and WO asks where — they swapped expectations exactly where English learners least expect. And German asks questions the way Early Modern English did: Kommst du? — 'Knowest thou?' Verb first, no do-support, no machinery.

footnotes.title: Romeo Spoke German
footnotes.content: warum is the structural twin of wherefore — wo (where) + um (for), 'for-what', exactly as wherefore is 'for-what'. Juliet's 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' asks WHY, not where — and warum asks the same question the same way.

pattern.title: The W-Grid and the Verb-First Flip
pattern.content:
The grid: was ↔ what, wo ↔ where, wer ↔ who, wann ↔ when, wie ↔ how (its root is why's — English split one ancient word into how and why; German's wie covers the how-job, warum the why-job), wohin ↔ whither (wo + hin, 'to where'). Questions build two ways: W-questions start with the W-word and keep the verb second — Wo ist der Kaffee? Wann kommst du? Yes/no questions flip the verb in front of the subject — Kommst du? Weißt du das? ist er da? No do, no auxiliary, just the ancient flip.

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Weißt du das? → Know you that? → Do you know that? The middle line is word-for-word German — verb flipped, no helper — and it was ordinary English not so long ago.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “questions need do.” German has no do in questions and never did — it flips subject and verb, exactly as English still does with can and must. Kann ich kommen? is Can I come? with nothing added at all.
pattern.linguist_note: English used to flip verbs too: 'Knowest thou?', 'Sawest thou him?' The do-support ('Do you know?') only spread in Early Modern English. German questions are the older machinery, still running.

exercises.prompt: Match the W-words with their English twins:
exercises.explanation: One family: English kept the h of the ancient hw-, German let it go.

exercises.prompt: The classic trap: which German word asks WHO?
exercises.explanation: wer ↔ who and wo ↔ where — the words swapped sound-shapes, not meanings. Trust the twins, not the looks.

exercises.idea: your friend said they might visit — ask it straight out: are you coming tomorrow?
cues: Yes/no questions flip the verb in front: kommst, then du
Add the time word at the end: morgen

vocab_hints.note: twin of 'morrow' — the word hiding inside to-morrow

exercises.explanation: The verb takes position 1 and the subject falls in behind — no do, no helper: 'Comest thou tomorrow?' in modern dress.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: A question word takes position 1, the verb takes position 2, and the subject follows. English uses do for this; German never needed it.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote the word order from the sound alone — wo, verb, subject, and no do anywhere.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.explanation: 'When come you?' is the German way: the verb flips in front of du, no helper needed. Modern English inserted do instead; German kept the ancient flip — 'Knowest thou?' was still good English in Shakespeare's day.

summary.outcome: Ask W-questions and verb-first yes/no questions with zero do-support.
summary.takeaway: The W-words are your W-words with the h shaved off — and German questions flip the verb like 'Knowest thou?'
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the w-word cognate set — all eight w-words matched to their English twins, wer≠where trap included.

twist.prompt: Same words, but now ask it: 'You know it.' Put the question into German — no do, just the flip.
twist.explanation: The verb takes position 1 and du falls in behind it — the ancient flip ('Knowest thou?'). The -st ending holds: weißt, like thou knowest.

wo.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwēr/*hwar — the exact twin of English where; English kept the h (wh-), German dropped it. [wiktionary]

wer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwaz — the exact twin of English who. The famous trap: wer asks WHO, wo asks WHERE. [wiktionary]

wann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when. [wiktionary]

wie.context_translation: How are you? (How goes it to you?)
wie.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hwē, a fossilized instrumental of who/what — the same variant that gave English why. [wiktionary]

warum.etymology_derivation: wo + um — 'around-what / for-what', the structural twin of English wherefore ('for what'). [wiktionary]

wohin.context_translation: Where are you going (whither goest thou)?
wohin.etymology_derivation: wo + hin; hin is the twin of the h- in English hence/hither — 'to where' in one word. [wiktionary]

ohr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ausô (Verner alternant) — the twin of English ear; Latin auris is PIE-kin. [wiktionary]

nein.context_translation: No, I do not have time.
nein.etymology_derivation: ni + ein, 'not one' — the same contraction story as English none/no from Old English nān. [wiktionary]

ernst.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ernust, Proto-Germanic *ernustuz; the English cognate is earnest, as in an earnest promise. [wiktionary]

kappe.context_phrase: Er setzt die Kappe auf den Kopf.
kappe.context_translation: He puts the cap on his head.
kappe.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German kappe, from Proto-West Germanic *kappā (coat, hood), a doublet of Kapuze - the same Late Latin cappa family as English cap. [wiktionary][etymonline]

tiger.context_translation: The tiger lives in the jungle.
tiger.etymology_derivation: The German entry derives Tiger only from the earlier compound Tigertier and gives no older chain. The identity with English tiger, from Greek tigris, is assumed here and flagged for human check. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

rezeption.context_phrase: Der Schlüssel ist an der Rezeption.
rezeption.context_translation: The key is at the reception desk.
rezeption.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin receptio — the same reception-word English uses for the hotel desk; both go back to the root of seize. [wiktionary]

fliehen.context_phrase: Die Familie flieht vor dem Feuer.
fliehen.context_translation: The family flees from the fire.
fliehen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną — English flee is the documented cognate (Old English flēon); German kept the old strong past floh, geflohen. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
